clinicalPearls: The most common genital anomaly in male infants, defined by failure of one or both testes to reach a normal scrotal position, and more frequent in preterm boys
It must be distinguished from a retractile testis, which can be manipulated into the scrotum and remains there, and which does not require surgery
Spontaneous descent may occur in the first months of life, but is unlikely after around 6 months of corrected age, after which surgical correction is planned
The undescended testis carries an increased lifetime risk of malignancy (typically a germ cell tumour) and of impaired fertility, particularly with bilateral or intra-abdominal testes

Bilateral non-palpable testes, especially with any genital ambiguity or hypospadias, may indicate a disorder of sex development or congenital adrenal hyperplasia and require urgent karyotype and hormonal evaluation
Orchidopexy, ideally performed in infancy, relocates and fixes the testis in the scrotum to optimise fertility potential and to allow easier examination for later malignancy
An acquired or ascending testis can present in an older boy whose testis was previously scrotal, and also warrants surgical correction
reference.pathophysiology: Testicular descent proceeds in two hormonally regulated phases: a transabdominal phase governed largely by insulin-like factor 3 acting on the gubernaculum, and an inguinoscrotal phase dependent on androgen action. Disruption of these processes, through hormonal, mechanical, or genetic factors, leaves the testis arrested along its normal path of descent, most often in the inguinal region. The abnormally high position exposes the testis to a warmer environment than the scrotum, which impairs germ cell maturation over time and contributes to reduced fertility, while the underlying developmental abnormality also predisposes to malignant change. Bilateral non-palpable testes may reflect anorchia, intra-abdominal testes, or an underlying disorder of sex development.
additionalDifferentials: Retractile testis (a normal variant due to an active cremasteric reflex)
Ectopic testis lying outside the normal line of descent
Disorder of sex development presenting with bilateral impalpable gonads
Congenital adrenal hyperplasia in an undervirilised or apparently 'cryptorchid' infant
additionalInvestigations: Careful, warm-handed physical examination to determine whether the testis is palpable and retractile
Karyotype and disorder-of-sex-development assessment when gonads are bilaterally impalpable or ambiguity is present
Serum LH, FSH, testosterone, and anti-Müllerian hormone/inhibin B to assess for testicular tissue
hCG stimulation test to detect functioning testicular tissue in bilateral non-palpable cases
Diagnostic laparoscopy to localise or confirm absence of an intra-abdominal testis
Adrenal hormone profile (including 17-hydroxyprogesterone) where congenital adrenal hyperplasia is a concern
redFlags: Bilateral non-palpable testes with any genital ambiguity, which may represent a virilised female with congenital adrenal hyperplasia and a salt-wasting risk
A previously descended testis that has ascended, requiring surgical referral
Acute pain and swelling in the region of an undescended testis suggesting torsion
A new inguinal or abdominal mass raising concern about malignant change
reference.prognosis: Early orchidopexy improves the outlook for fertility and facilitates surveillance, but an increased relative risk of testicular malignancy persists and fertility is lower with bilateral or intra-abdominal disease; unilateral corrected cryptorchidism is generally compatible with normal paternity.
pitfalls: Mistaking a retractile testis for a truly undescended one and performing unnecessary surgery
Failing to recognise bilateral impalpable testes as a potential endocrine and disorder-of-sex-development emergency
Deferring orchidopexy well beyond infancy and losing the fertility and surveillance benefits of early correction
Relying on imaging to 'find' an impalpable testis rather than proceeding to laparoscopy
Overlooking an acquired ascending testis in an older boy assumed to have been treated
management: Orchidopexy to mobilise and fix the testis in the scrotum, ideally performed in infancy once spontaneous descent is no longer expected
Diagnostic laparoscopy to localise an impalpable testis, with a single-stage or staged Fowler-Stephens orchidopexy for an intra-abdominal testis
Distinguish a retractile testis, which is observed rather than operated on
Urgent karyotype and endocrine evaluation for bilateral impalpable testes or associated genital ambiguity to exclude a disorder of sex development or congenital adrenal hyperplasia
Long-term counselling on fertility and teaching of testicular self-examination given the raised risk of germ cell tumour
Refer to paediatric surgery or urology, with paediatric endocrinology and clinical genetics input when a disorder of sex development is suspected
